name: Rio de Janeiro
info: Rio de Janeiro is a city on the Atlantic coast of south-eastern Brazil, at the entrance to Guanabara Bay, founded by the Portuguese in 1565 and for almost two centuries a colonial, royal, imperial and republican capital.

facts.founded: Founded on 1 March 1565 by the Portuguese, led by Estácio de Sá, as São Sebastião do Rio de Janeiro; Europeans had first reached Guanabara Bay on 1 January 1502.
facts.where: On the Atlantic coast of south-eastern Brazil, at the entrance to Guanabara Bay, marked by Sugar Loaf, in the state of Rio de Janeiro.
facts.known: The French colony of France Antarctique and its expulsion; the colonial port for Minas Gerais gold; the Valongo Wharf and the slave trade; seat of the Portuguese court from 1808; capital of the Empire and then of the Republic of Brazil until 1960; Carnival, samba and bossa nova
facts.today: Rio de Janeiro is the capital and largest city of the state of Rio de Janeiro and the second-largest city in Brazil after São Paulo.

t: The Portuguese founded Rio in 1565 after driving out a French colony on an island in Guanabara Bay, and the city became the colonial capital in 1763, when the administration moved from Salvador.
In 1808 the Portuguese royal court fled Napoleon's invasion and settled in Rio, which stayed the capital through the Empire of Brazil and the Republic until Brasília replaced it in 1960.
Rio was a city of enslaved people: between 1811 and 1831 half a million to a million enslaved people arrived through the Valongo Wharf, and its port was the largest slave port in the Americas.
dyk: When the Portuguese court arrived in 1808, Rio became the only European capital outside Europe, and many of its inhabitants were evicted from their homes to house the arriving nobles.
ev: A Portuguese expedition reaches Guanabara Bay on 1 January and gives the place its name
French colonists under Villegaignon occupy an island in the bay and found France Antarctique

Mayor Pereira Passos begins the reforms that rebuild the city centre

sections.origins:
Rio de Janeiro stands on a stretch of Brazil's Atlantic coast close to the Tropic of Capricorn, where the shoreline runs east and west, so that the city faces largely south. It was founded at the entrance to Guanabara Bay, which is marked by a point of land called Sugar Loaf. The region was inhabited by the Tupi, Puri, Botocudo and Maxakalí peoples, and before European colonisation there were at least seven different indigenous peoples speaking 20 languages in it.

Europeans first reached the bay on 1 January 1502, hence the name Rio de Janeiro, "January River", which was first the name of the bay. The expedition was led by Gaspar de Lemos, captain of a ship in Pedro Álvares Cabral's fleet, or by Gonçalo Coelho, and Amerigo Vespucci is said to have taken part as an observer. According to a legend the mariners took the mouth of the bay for the mouth of a river, but at the time "river" was the general word for any large body of water.

In 1555 about 500 French colonists under Admiral Nicolas Durand de Villegaignon occupied an island in the bay, now called Villegagnon Island, and built Fort Coligny there in an attempt to found the colony of France Antarctique. In 1560 the Portuguese ordered it removed, and a campaign led by Mem de Sá and then by his nephew Estácio de Sá ended on 20 January 1567 with the French forces' final defeat. The city itself was founded on 1 March 1565 by the Portuguese under Estácio de Sá, with Antônio de Mariz among them, and named São Sebastião do Rio de Janeiro in honour of St Sebastian, the namesake and patron of the Portuguese king Sebastião.
sections.growth:
The city became far more useful when gold and diamonds were found in the neighbouring captaincy of Minas Gerais, because Rio was a more practical port than Salvador, much farther to the north-east, for exporting gold, precious stones and sugar. On 27 January 1763 the colonial administration of Portuguese America moved from Salvador to Rio.

The arrival of the Portuguese court in 1808 changed the city. In the first decade several educational establishments were created, among them the Military Academy, the Royal School of Sciences, Arts and Crafts and the Imperial Academy of Fine Arts, together with the National Library of Brazil and the Botanical Garden. The Gazeta do Rio de Janeiro, the first printed newspaper in Brazil, appeared in the same period. After independence the empire was enriched by sugar cane in the Campos region and by coffee in the Paraíba Valley. In the second half of the 19th century the city gained modern drains, animal-drawn trams, railway stations, gas and electric lighting, and telephone and telegraph wires.

Until the early 20th century the city was largely limited to the area now called the historic centre, at the mouth of the bay. Its centre of gravity then began to shift south and west when the first tunnel was built under the mountains between Botafogo and Copacabana, and the consolidation and electrification of the streetcar system after 1905 helped the city to expand north and south. In 1890 the native-born Portuguese and their children numbered 267,664, or 51.2 per cent of the inhabitants of Rio.
sections.rulers:
Rio began as the seat of the Captaincy of Rio de Janeiro, a domain of the Portuguese Empire. In 1763 it became the capital of the State of Brazil, and it remained primarily a colonial capital until 1808, when the Portuguese royal family and most of the Lisbon nobles moved to the city to escape Napoleon's invasion of Portugal. Rio became the seat of the court of Queen Maria I, and her son, the Prince Regent John, raised Brazil to the dignity of a kingdom within the United Kingdom of Portugal, Brazil and the Algarves in 1815. The royal family returned to Lisbon in 1821, but Rio stayed the capital of the Kingdom of Brazil. This was the only instance in modern history in which the capital of a colonising country officially shifted to a city in one of its colonies.

When Prince Pedro proclaimed the independence of Brazil in 1822 he kept Rio as the capital of his new empire. In 1834 the city was made a Neutral Municipality, to separate it from the province of Rio de Janeiro, whose capital became Niterói. Rio continued as the capital after the monarchy was replaced by a republic in 1889.

On 21 April 1960 the capital was officially moved to Brasília, which President Juscelino Kubitschek had built. The former Federal District became the state of Guanabara, covering only the city, which after the military coup of 1964 was the only state left in Brazil to oppose the dictatorship. In 1975 a presidential decree known as "The Fusion" removed its federative status and merged it with the state of Rio de Janeiro, of which the city then became the capital in place of Niterói.
sections.life:
From the colonial period to the first years of independence Rio was a city of enslaved people. A large number of enslaved people were brought to it from Africa: in 1819 there were 145,000 enslaved people in the captaincy, and by 1840 there were 220,000. Between 1811 and 1831, 500,000 to a million enslaved people arrived in Rio through the Valongo Wharf, now a World Heritage Site, and the port of Rio de Janeiro was the largest slave port in the Americas. The city's Black community was formed by people trafficked into slavery, mostly from Angola and Mozambique. In the last half of the 19th century Rio was the main stage of the abolitionist and republican movements, and the number of enslaved people was drastically reduced.

Many immigrants came after independence, among them hundreds of thousands from Portugal, mostly poor peasants who found prosperity as city workers and small traders. The census of 1920 showed that 39.7 per cent of the Portuguese living in Brazil lived in Rio. Muslim, Jewish and Maronite Christian immigrants from the Ottoman Empire settled around Rua da Alfândega in the early 20th century. Catholicism is the majority religion, with Saint Sebastian as the city's patron saint, and many people also observe Afro-Brazilian religions such as Umbanda and Candomblé. Carnival, which is held before Lent, had its first masked ball in 1840; it was long a high-class event led by white people, and the influence of African-Brazilian drums and music became more noticeable from the first half of the 20th century.
sections.crises:
The indigenous peoples of the bay were drawn into the struggle over the French settlement. Some joined the Portuguese and others the French; the Portuguese then exterminated those who had joined the French, and the rest were assimilated. Until early in the 18th century French pirates and buccaneers threatened or invaded the city, among them Jean-François Duclerc and René Duguay-Trouin. When the court arrived in 1808 there was no space for the hundreds of noblemen who came, and many inhabitants were evicted from their homes.

When the Old Republic was established the city lacked urban planning and sanitation, which helped spread yellow fever, dysentery, smallpox, tuberculosis and even plague. Pereira Passos, mayor from 1902, modernised the city by demolishing the cortiços, where most of the poor lived; they moved to the hills and created the first favelas. Inspired by Paris, Passos built the Municipal Theatre, the National Museum of Fine Arts and the National Library, and named Oswaldo Cruz director general of public health. Cruz's plan against disease included compulsory vaccination of the whole population and forced entry into houses to kill mosquitoes and rats, and the people rebelled in the Vaccine Revolt.

In 1910 Afro-Brazilian crew members of the Brazilian Navy mutinied in the Revolt of the Lash against the heavy corporal punishment, which resembled that of enslaved people; they took the battleship Minas Geraes and threatened to fire on the city. The Copacabana Fort revolt of 1922 marched against the Old Republic's coronelism and began Tenentism.
sections.legacy:
After 1960 about a third of all federal public bodies and companies remained in Rio, among them the National Library, Fiocruz, BNDES and Petrobras, and more than half of the federal civil servants of the Executive branch stayed in the city. Many of its older institutions date from the court's years or the empire: the National Library with the largest collection in Latin America, the Botanical Garden and the Passeio Público, the first public park in the Americas. Tijuca National Park has been a national park since 1961.

Rio is the home of samba and bossa nova, which was born there, and its samba schools parade in the Sambódromo during Carnival. The Valongo Wharf, where so many enslaved people landed, is a World Heritage Site, and the city's arts, urban culture and designed landscapes set around the natural environment have also been inscribed by UNESCO. The old centre keeps the Paço Imperial, built for the Portuguese governors, and the churches and monasteries of the colonial city, while the Belle Époque buildings around Cinelândia date from the early 20th century.

Rio de Janeiro is today the capital and largest city of the state of Rio de Janeiro and the second-largest city in Brazil after São Paulo, which passed it in 1960. About 6 million people live in the city proper and about 13 million in its metropolitan area. Its residents are called cariocas, and its official song is "Cidade Maravilhosa".

summary: Rio de Janeiro was founded by the Portuguese in 1565 at the entrance to Guanabara Bay. It became the colonial capital in 1763, the seat of the Portuguese court from 1808, and the capital of the Empire and the Republic of Brazil until 1960. Its port was the largest slave port in the Americas.
notes: FIRST SIGHTING: the two articles differ. The main article says the expedition was under Gaspar de Lemos or Gonçalo Coelho, with Vespucci allegedly an observer; the History article says it was under Vespucci and included Lemos. I followed the main article's hedge and gave both leaders.
GOLD IN MINAS GERAIS: the main article says gold and diamonds were found in the late 17th century; the History article says the Portuguese found them after 1720. I left the date out.

CAPITAL BEFORE 1763: the main article's federal-government section says Rio was capital of the State of Brazil from 1621 to 1815 and gives 1889-1968 for the republic; the History section says 1763 and 1960. I used 1763 and 1960 and left the others out.

The History article says the city was 'founded' on 1 March 1565; the main article names Estácio de Sá and Antônio de Mariz. I used the main article. The final expulsion of the French (20 January 1567) is from the main article only.
The History article says Portuguese land exploration found 'several years after' first exploring Brazil French traders came; I kept it vague ('soon afterwards') rather than dating it.

TUPI: the main article lists Tupi, Puri, Botocudo and Maxakalí but does not say which peoples joined the French or the Portuguese, nor the Tupi's name for the bay; I did not add either. The statement that the Portuguese 'exterminated' the peoples allied with the French is the article's word and is kept as written.

SLAVERY FIGURES: 145,000 (1819, captaincy), 220,000 (1840, no area given), and 500,000 to a million through Valongo Wharf 1811-1831, as the article gives them; the 220,000 is not stated to be of the captaincy, so the text says only 'by 1840 there were 220,000'. 'Mostly from Angola and Mozambique' describes the origin of the Black community as the article does. The article gives no figure for Rio's enslaved population in the city itself.
'Largest slave port in America' is the article's wording; I wrote 'in the Americas'.
Plague is listed among diseases as 'black death' in the article; I wrote plague. Smallpox for 'variola'.

Tijuca National Park: the article says both 'the second largest urban forest in the world' and 'the world's first urban forest'; and calls the Pedra Branca forest the largest. I used only the 'second largest' wording as 'described as'.

'More than half of the federal civil servants': the article says 59% of Executive Branch civil servants of federal agencies and public companies remained in the city; I wrote 'more than half'. The 'about a third of all federal public bodies' is as given.

The article says the first favelas arose when Passos's demolitions pushed the poor to the hills; I told it as the article does. Later figures for favelas (813, 21%) and police killings are undated or recent and were left out.
Left out as tourism, sport, economy or present government: beaches, Christ the Redeemer, Olympics, World Cups, GDP, universities, crime, climate and pollution detail, twin towns.

Population: 6 million city proper and 13 million metropolitan area, given 'as of 2025' in the article; written without the year as the guide asks. The 1890 figure (267,664, 51.2%) is the article's; it is the only population figure of an earlier date.
The article's Rock in Rio, football at Bangu and the 2009 DNA study were left out.
